Chapter 2: The Danger of a Diminished View of God
There’s a quiet crisis that most of us never notice. It doesn’t grab headlines, and you probably won’t hear anyone debating it on TV. But its effects? They’re all around us—in conversations about faith, in the choices people make, and in the struggles they quietly carry.
Here’s what’s really going on: when we shrink our idea of God, everything else in life gets smaller too.
Think about a teacher who used to find deep meaning in her work. For her, the classroom was more than just a place to teach—it was a space where she sensed God’s presence, where every lesson felt like an act of worship. But as time went on and the pressures of daily life piled up, that sense of God’s nearness faded. The focus shifted to test scores and routines. The work lost its spark, and the joy quietly slipped away.
This isn’t just one person’s story, or something that only happens to teachers. It’s a pattern that repeats itself in so many different ways. When we start to see God as distant, or uninvolved in our lives, faith becomes a private thing—something we keep tucked away and separate from everything else. People start relying on their own strength, chasing after security and success, measuring their worth by what’s visible and what can be counted.
Most of the time, we don’t even realize how much this shift affects us. It’s easy to think that what we believe about God is just one part of life—something that belongs in its own little box. But the truth? Every decision, every hope, every fear is shaped by what we believe about God. When God seems small, our problems loom larger, and the world feels a lot more threatening. When God feels distant, loneliness grows, and our hearts become restless.
Sometimes we try to fill that gap with more activity—more meetings, more programs, more noise. But let’s be honest, those efforts rarely satisfy for long. The real need goes much deeper. What we’re longing for is a vision of God that’s actually worthy of worship—a God who’s both close and beyond us, both loving and holy.
This kind of faith isn’t born from clever arguments or a rush of emotion. It’s about seeing God as He truly is.
There’s a story about a parent who, after years of striving, finally admitted that something was missing. The routines were in place, the family was cared for, but that sense of God’s presence? It was gone. In a rare moment of honesty, the parent realized the problem wasn’t really the circumstances—it was the way God had been imagined. The God who once inspired awe had faded into the background, useful but not essential.
Here’s something to pay attention to: our deepest need isn’t for more information, or better techniques. What we need most is a new vision of God’s greatness. When we see God as He truly is, everything else falls into place. Worries get smaller. Hope grows. Life takes on a whole new meaning.
And the journey back to awe? It doesn’t require something dramatic. It just starts with a quiet act of humility—admitting that maybe our view of God has grown too small, and being willing to see Him with fresh eyes.
